claim: Participants reached 95% of maximal skill within the initial 11 practice trials during early learning.
source: Participants reached 95% of maximal skill (i.e., - Early Learning) within the initial 11 practice trials (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B, which displays the learning curve.

claim: Improvements during early learning developed over inter-practice rest periods (micro-offline gains) accounting for almost all total learning across participants.
source: with improvements developing over inter-practice rest periods (micro-offline gains) accounting for almost all total learning across participants (Figure 1B, inset; Bönstrup et al., 2019a)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B inset and cited from previous work (Bönstrup et al., 2019a).

claim: At the group level, total early learning was exclusively accounted for by micro-offline gains during inter-practice rest intervals.
source: At the group level, total early learning was exclusively accounted for by micro-offline gains during inter-practice rest intervals (B, inset; F [2,75]=14.79, p=3.86 × 10–6; micro-online vs. micro-offline: p=7.98 × 10–6; micro-online vs. total: p=0.0002; micro-offline vs. total: p=0.669)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) with specific F-statistic and p-values provided.

claim: Individual keypress transition times became more consistent across repeated sequence iterations during early learning.
source: In addition to the reduction in sequence duration during early learning, individual keypress transition times became more consistent across repeated sequence iterations (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data visualization in Figure 1C showing keypress transition time variability.

claim: On average across subjects, 2.32% ± 1.48% (mean ± SD) of all keypresses performed were errors.
source: On average across subjects, 2.32% ± 1.48% (mean ± SD) of all keypresses performed were errors, which were evenly distributed across the four possible keypress responses.
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative data about error rates during the task.

claim: An upward shift in performance of the trained sequence (0.68 ± SD 0.56 keypresses/s; t=7.21, p<0.001) was observed during Day 2 Retest, indicative of an overnight skill consolidation effect.
source: As expected, an upward shift in performance of the trained sequence (0.68 ± SD 0.56 keypresses/s; t=7.21, p<0.001) was observed during Day 2 Retest, indicative of an overnight skill consolidation effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) with specific values and references to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Decoders trained on broadband activity consistently outperformed those trained on narrowband activity.
source: We found that decoders trained on broadband activity consistently outperformed those trained on narrowband activity.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of decoder performance across different frequency bands.

claim: Whole-brain parcel-space decoders exhibited 70.11% ± SD 7.11% accuracy.
source: Whole-brain parcel-space (70.11% ± SD 7.11% accuracy; n=148 brain regions; t=1.89, p=0.035, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.17, Figure 2A; also see Figure 2B for topographic map of feature importance scores)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative accuracy data with statistical measures.

claim: Whole-brain voxel-space decoders exhibited 74.51% ± SD 7.34% accuracy.
source: voxel-space (74.51% ± SD 7.34% accuracy; n=15684; t=7.18, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.76, Figure 2A; also see Figure 2C for topographic map of feature importance scores; Destrieux et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative accuracy data with statistical measures and citation.

claim: Optimal decoding required information from multiple brain regions, predominantly contralateral to the hand engaged in the skill task.
source: Thus, optimal decoding required information from multiple brain regions, predominantly contralateral to the hand engaged in the skill task (Figure 2B and C)
evidence: The claim is supported by feature importance maps shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Hybrid-space decoders achieved accuracy of 78.15% ± SD 7.03% (weighted mean F1 score of 0.78 ± SD 0.07).
source: Accuracy was higher for hybrid- (78.15% ± SD 7.03%; weighted mean F1 score of 0.78 ± SD 0.07)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative accuracy and F1 score data.

claim: Hybrid-space decoder accuracy was significantly higher than voxel-space decoder accuracy (paired t-test: t=6.30, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.39).
source: than for voxel- (74.51% ± SD 7.34%; paired t-test: t=6.30, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.39)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison using paired t-test.

claim: Hybrid-space decoder accuracy was significantly higher than parcel-space decoder accuracy (paired t-test: t=12.08, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.98).
source: and parcel-space decoders (70.11% ± SD 7.48%; paired t-test: t=12.08, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.98, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison using paired t-test.

claim: A multi-scale hybrid-space representation best characterizes the keypress action manifolds.
source: Thus, a multi-scale hybrid-space representation best characterizes the keypress action manifolds.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the superior performance of hybrid-space decoders.

claim: LDA-based manifold extraction led to the greatest classifier performance gains, improving keypress decoding accuracy to 90.47% ± SD 3.44%.
source: LDA-based manifold extraction led to the greatest classifier performance gains, improving keypress decoding accuracy to 90.47% ± SD 3.44% (Figure 3B; weighted mean F1 score = 0.91 ± SD 0.05)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative accuracy data after applying LDA dimensionality reduction.

claim: Index finger keypresses exhibited the highest false negative (0.115 per keypress) and false positive (0.067 per prediction) misclassification rates compared with all other digits.
source: Notably, decoding of index finger keypresses (executed at two different ordinal positions in the sequence) exhibited the highest false negative (0.115 per keypress) and false positive (0.067 per prediction) misclassification rates compared with all other digits (false negative rate range = [0.067 0.114]; false positive rate range = [0.085 0.131]; Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative misclassification rates from the confusion matrix.

claim: The decoding accuracy for Day 2 MEG data remained high (87.11% ± SD 8.54% for the trained sequence during Retest, and 79.44% ± SD 5.54% for the untrained Control sequences).
source: The decoding accuracy for Day 2 MEG data remained high (87.11% ± SD 8.54% for the trained sequence during Retest, and 79.44% ± SD 5.54% for the untrained Control sequences; Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative accuracy data for Day 2 testing.

claim: Index finger classifiers constructed using the hybrid decoding approach robustly generalized from Day 1 to Day 2 across trained and untrained keypress sequences.
source: Thus, index finger classifiers constructed using the hybrid decoding approach robustly generalized from Day 1 to Day 2 across trained and untrained keypress sequences.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high decoding accuracy maintained on Day 2.

claim: Within-subject keypress neural representations progressively differentiated during early learning.
source: Within-subject keypress neural representations progressively differentiated during early learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by visualization of neural representation clustering over trials.

claim: The cortical representation of keypress clusters changed over the course of training, beginning with predominant involvement of contralateral pre-central areas in trial 1 before transitioning to greater contralateral post-central, superior frontal, and middle frontal cortex contributions in trials 11 and 36.
source: The cortical representation of these clusters changed over the course of training, beginning with predominant involvement of contralateral pre-central areas in trial 1 before transitioning to greater contralateral post-central, superior frontal, and middle frontal cortex contributions in trials 11 and 36 (Figure 4A, bottom row)
evidence: The claim is supported by feature importance maps shown in Figure 4A bottom row.

claim: Inclusion of sequence location information for each keypress improved decoding accuracy from 90.47% (± SD 3.44%) to 94.15% (± SD 4.84%; weighted mean F1 score: 0.94).
source: Inclusion of sequence location information (i.e. sequence context) for each keypress action (five sequence elements with the one keypress represented twice at two different locations) improved decoding accuracy (t=7.09, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.86, Figure 4B) from 90.47% (± SD 3.44%) to 94.15% (± SD 4.84%; weighted mean F1 score: 0.94)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) showing improved accuracy with contextual information.

claim: The improved decoding accuracy is supported by greater differentiation in neural representations of the index finger keypresses performed at positions 1 and 5 of the sequence.
source: The improved decoding accuracy is supported by greater differentiation in neural representations of the index finger keypresses performed at positions 1 and 5 of the sequence (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by visualization in Figure 4A showing sub-clustering of index finger representations.

claim: The trial-by-trial increase in 2-class decoding accuracy over early learning was observed across different decoder window durations.
source: and by the trial-by-trial increase in 2-class decoding accuracy over early learning (Figure 4C) across different decoder window durations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: On Day 2, incorporating contextual information into the hybrid-space decoder enhanced classification accuracy for the trained sequence only (improving from 87.11% for 4-class to 90.22% for 5-class), while performing at or below-chance levels for the control sequences (≤30.22% ± SD 0.44%).
source: On Day 2, incorporating contextual information into the hybrid-space decoder enhanced classification accuracy for the trained sequence only (improving from 87.11% for 4-class to 90.22% for 5-class), while performing at or below-chance levels for the control sequences (≤30.22% ± SD 0.44%)
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative accuracy data showing specificity of contextual decoding to the trained sequence.

claim: The accuracy improvements resulting from inclusion of contextual information in the decoding framework were specific to the trained skill sequence.
source: Thus, the accuracy improvements resulting from inclusion of contextual information in the decoding framework were specific to the trained skill sequence.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential performance on trained vs. control sequences.

claim: Both online and offline contextualization between the two index finger representations increases sharply over Early Learning before stabilizing across later Day 1 Training trials.
source: Both online and offline contextualization between the two index finger representations increases sharply over Early Learning before stabilizing across later Day 1 Training trials.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The cumulative neural representation differences during early learning were significantly greater over rest (Offline contextualization) than during practice (Online contextualization) periods (t=4.84, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=1.2).
source: The cumulative neural representation differences during early learning were significantly greater over rest (Offline contextualization; right) than during practice (Online contextualization; left) periods (t=4.84, p<0.001, df = 25, Cohen's d=1.2)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (t-test) between offline and online contextualization.

claim: Offline contextualization strongly correlated with cumulative micro-offline gains (r=0.903, R²=0.816, p<0.001).
source: Offline contextualization strongly correlated with cumulative micro-offline gains (r=0.903, R²=0.816, p<0.001; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, inset)
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis showing strong correlation.

claim: Online contextualization (using either measurement approach) did not explain early online learning gains.
source: Conversely, online contextualization (using either measurement approach) did not explain early online learning gains (i.e. Figure 5—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by lack of correlation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The average correlation between offline contextualization and micro-offline gains within individuals was significantly greater than zero (t=3.87, p=0.00035, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.76).
source: The average correlation between offline contextualization and micro-offline gains within individuals was significantly greater than zero (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, left; t=3.87, p=0.00035, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.76)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of within-subject correlations.

claim: The average correlation between offline contextualization and micro-offline gains was stronger than correlations between online contextualization and either micro-online (t=3.28, p=0.0015, df = 25, Cohen's d=1.2) or micro-offline gains (t=3.7021, p=5.3013e-04, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.69).
source: and stronger than correlations between online contextualization and either micro-online (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, middle; t=3.28, p=0.0015, df = 25, Cohen's d=1.2) or micro-offline gains (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, right; t=3.7021, p=5.3013e-04, df = 25, Cohen's d=0.69)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) of within-subject correlations.

claim: Contextualization findings were not explained by behavioral changes of typing rhythm (t=–0.03, p=0.976).
source: These findings were not explained by behavioral changes of typing rhythm (t=–0.03, p=0.976; Figure 5—figure supplement 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant relationship with typing rhythm.

claim: Contextualization findings were not explained by adjacent keypress transition times (R2=0.00507, F [1,3202]=16.3).
source: adjacent keypress transition times (R2=0.00507, F [1,3202]=16.3; Figure 5—figure supplement 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis showing very weak relationship with keypress transition times.

claim: Contextualization findings were not explained by overall typing speed (between-subject; R2=0.028, p=0.41).
source: or overall typing speed (between-subject; R2=0.028, p=0.41; Figure 5—figure supplement 7)
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis showing no significant relationship with typing speed.

claim: Contextualization of IndexOP1 vs. IndexOP5 representations observed on Day 1 generalized to Day 2 Retest of the trained skill sequence.
source: Finally, contextualization of IndexOP1 vs. IndexOP5 representations observed on Day 1 generalized to Day 2 Retest of the trained skill sequence.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Distances between representations for the same keypress performed twice within untrained sequences were lower in magnitude (Day 2 Control)—pointing to specificity of the contextualization effect.
source: Distances between representations for the same keypress performed twice within untrained sequences were lower in magnitude (Day 2 Control)—pointing to specificity of the contextualization effect (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of contextualization measures between trained and control sequences shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Individual sequence action representations differentiate during early skill learning in a manner reflecting the local sequence context in which they were performed.
source: The main findings of this study during which subjects engaged in a naturalistic, self-paced task were that individual sequence action representations differentiate during early skill learning in a manner reflecting the local sequence context in which they were performed
evidence: This is the main finding summarizing the overall results of the study.

claim: The degree of representational differentiation—particularly prominent over rest intervals—correlated with skill gains.
source: and that the degree of representational differentiation—particularly prominent over rest intervals—correlated with skill gains.
evidence: This is the main finding summarizing the correlation between contextualization and learning.

claim: The neural substrates supporting finger movements and their representational differentiation during early skill learning (trials 1–11) differed from those supporting stable performance during the subsequent skill plateau period (trials 12–36).
source: Thus, the neural substrates supporting finger movements and their representational differentiation during early skill learning (the time period during which 95% skill gains in the training session occur Bönstrup et al., 2019a; Pan and Rickard, 2015, trials 1–11 in this study) differed from those supporting stable performance during the subsequent skill plateau period (Karni et al., 1995; Robertson and Cohen, 2006; trials 12–36 in this study)
evidence: The claim is supported by the shift in feature importance from pre-central to frontal regions and cited literature.

claim: Micro-offline gains observed during early learning are reproducible.
source: Micro-offline gains observed during early learning are reproducible (Jacobacci et al., 2020; Brooks et al., 2024; Bönstrup et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2024; Sjøgård, 2024)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Micro-offline gains are similar in magnitude even when practice periods are reduced by half to 5 seconds in length, thereby confirming that they are not merely a result of recovery from performance fatigue.
source: and are similar in magnitude even when practice periods are reduced by half to 5 seconds in length, thereby confirming that they are not merely a result of recovery from performance fatigue (Bönstrup et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work that tested shorter practice periods.

claim: Micro-offline gains are unaffected by the random termination of practice periods, which eliminates the possibility of predictive motor slowing as a contributing factor.
source: Additionally, they are unaffected by the random termination of practice periods, which eliminates the possibility of predictive motor slowing as a contributing factor (Bönstrup et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work that tested random termination.

claim: Micro-offline gains during early learning represent a form of memory consolidation.
source: Collectively, these behavioral findings point towards the interpretation that micro-offline gains during early learning represent a form of memory consolidation (Bönstrup et al., 2019a)
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on behavioral findings and cited literature.

claim: In humans, the rate of hippocampo-neocortical neural replay predicts micro-offline gains.
source: In humans, the rate of hippocampo-neocortical neural replay predicts micro-offline gains (Buch et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chen et al., 2024 and Sjøgård, 2024 furnished direct evidence from intracranial human EEG studies, demonstrating a connection between the density of hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (80–120 Hz) and micro-offline gains during early learning.
source: Consistent with these findings, Chen et al., 2024 and Sjøgård, 2024 furnished direct evidence from intracranial human EEG studies, demonstrating a connection between the density of hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (80–120 Hz)—recognized markers of neural replay—and micro-offline gains during early learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent intracranial EEG studies.

claim: Griffin et al. reported that neural replay of task-related ensembles in the motor cortex of macaques during brief rest periods is not merely correlated with, but are causal drivers of micro-offline learning.
source: Further, Griffin et al. reported that neural replay of task-related ensembles in the motor cortex of macaques during brief rest periods—akin to those observed in humans (Bönstrup et al., 2019a; Buch et al., 2021; Jacobacci et al., 2020; Mylonas et al., 2024; Wamsley et al., 2023)—is not merely correlated with, but are causal drivers of micro-offline learning (Griffin et al., 2025)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study in non-human primates.

claim: The same reach directions that were replayed the most during rest breaks showed the greatest reduction in path length during subsequent trials.
source: Specifically, the same reach directions that were replayed the most during rest breaks showed the greatest reduction in path length (i.e. more efficient movement path between two locations in the reach sequence) during subsequent trials
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2025.

claim: Stimulation applied during rest intervals preceding performance plateau reduced reactivation rates and virtually abolished micro-offline gains.
source: while stimulation applied during rest intervals preceding performance plateau reduced reactivation rates and virtually abolished micro-offline gains (Griffin et al., 2025)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2025 showing causal evidence.

claim: After a skill is learned over extended periods (i.e. weeks), the neural representation of the sequence changes significantly.
source: After a skill is learned over extended periods (i.e. weeks), the neural representation of the sequence changes significantly (Yokoi and Diedrichsen, 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on long-term learning.

claim: After a skill is learned over extended periods, the representation of its individual action components (e.g. finger movements) does not change.
source: while the representation of its individual action components (e.g. finger movements) does not (Beukema et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is not known whether individual sequence action representations differentiate or remain stable during the early stages of skill learning, when the memory is still not fully formed.
source: On the other hand, it is not known whether individual sequence action representations differentiate or remain stable during the early stages of skill learning, when the memory is still not fully formed (Bönstrup et al., 2019a)
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: It is unknown whether the neural representations of identical movements, performed at different positions within a skill sequence (i.e. the skill context), differentiate with learning.
source: Furthermore, it is unknown whether the neural representations of identical movements, performed at different positions within a skill sequence (i.e. the skill context), differentiate with learning—an important consideration for advancing robust brain-computer interface (BCI) applications (Merino et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap and cites relevant BCI literature.

claim: Low-frequency oscillations (LFOs) result in higher decoding accuracy compared to other narrow-band activity.
source: Evaluation of individual brain oscillatory activity revealed that low-frequency oscillations (LFOs) result in higher decoding accuracy compared to other narrow-band activity (Natraj et al., 2022; Reddy et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the current study and citations to previous work.

claim: LFOs, observed during movement onset in the cerebral cortex of animals and humans, encode information about movement trajectories and velocity.
source: LFOs, observed during movement onset in the cerebral cortex of animals (Bansal et al., 2011; Mollazadeh et al., 2011) and humans (Bönstrup et al., 2019b; Cruikshank et al., 2012; Tomassini et al., 2017), encode information about movement trajectories and velocity (Bansal et al., 2011; Mollazadeh et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: LFOs contain information related to movement timing, preparation, sensorimotor integration, and kinematics.
source: They also contain information related to movement timing (Ramanathan et al., 2018; Hall et al., 2014; Stefanics et al., 2010), preparation (Flint et al., 2012; Krasoulis et al., 2014), sensorimotor integration (Cruikshank et al., 2012), kinematics (Flint et al., 2012; Krasoulis et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: LFOs may contribute to the precise temporal coordination of movements required for sequencing.
source: and may contribute to the precise temporal coordination of movements required for sequencing (Churchland et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citation.

claim: Within clinical contexts, LFOs in the frontoparietal regions have been linked to recovery of motor function after brain lesions like stroke.
source: Within clinical contexts, LFOs in the frontoparietal regions, resulting in high decoding accuracy in the present study, have been linked to recovery of motor function after brain lesions like stroke (Bönstrup et al., 2019b; Ramanathan et al., 2018; Frohlich et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: A possible neural mechanism supporting contextualization could be the emergence and stabilization of conjunctive 'what–where' representations of procedural memories.
source: A possible neural mechanism supporting contextualization could be the emergence and stabilization of conjunctive 'what–where' representations of procedural memories (Komorowski et al., 2009) with the corresponding modulation of neuronal population dynamics (Georgopoulos, 1994; Georgopoulos et al., 1982) during early learning.
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The systematic inclusion of contextualized information into sequence skill practice environments could improve learning in areas as diverse as music education, sports training, and rehabilitation of motor skills after brain lesions.
source: It is possible that the systematic inclusion of contextualized information into sequence skill practice environments could improve learning in areas as diverse as music education, sports training, and rehabilitation of motor skills after brain lesions.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The study was approved by the Combined Neuroscience Institutional Review Board of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
source: The study was approved by the Combined Neuroscience Institutional Review Board of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
evidence: The claim states the ethical approval for the study.

claim: A total of thirty-three young and healthy adults (16 females) with a mean age of 26.6 years (±0.87 SEM) participated in the study.
source: A total of thirty-three young and healthy adults (16 females) with a mean age of 26.6 years (±0.87 SEM) participated in the study after providing written informed consent and undergoing a standard neurological examination.
evidence: The claim provides demographic information about study participants.

claim: Two participants were excluded from the analysis due to MEG system malfunction during data acquisition.
source: Two participants were excluded from the analysis due to MEG system malfunction during data acquisition.
evidence: The claim describes exclusion criteria applied to the dataset.

claim: An additional 5 subjects were excluded because they failed to generate any correct sequences in two or more consecutive trials.
source: An additional 5 subjects were excluded because they failed to generate any correct sequences in two or more consecutive trials.
evidence: The claim describes exclusion criteria applied to the dataset.

claim: The included study sample size (n=26) exceeded the calculated minimum sample size of 22.
source: The calculated minimum sample size was 22. The included study sample size (n=26) exceeded this minimum (Bönstrup et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim describes the power analysis and final sample size.

claim: The mean measured head movement across the study group was 1.159 mm (±1.077 SD).
source: The mean measured head movement across the study group was 1.159 mm (±1.077 SD; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim provides quantitative data about head movement during MEG recording.
